items.lesson_title: Enforcing Least Privilege in Recursive Delegation via Scope Attenuation
items.stem: A distribution agent can read inventory, create shipping labels and release payments. It delegates label creation to a contractor agent. The issuer is offline, but the token supports offline attenuation and the contractor can reach the label API. Which credential should the distribution agent give the contractor?

options.a: The original token with an instruction to call only the label API.
options.b: A new token from the contractor that can create labels and read inventory.
options.c: A derived token whose effective permission only allows creating labels.
options.d: A copy of the original token with a shorter lifetime and all three permissions.

items.rationale: The contractor needs only label creation. Offline attenuation can restrict the effective permissions of a derived credential without contacting the issuer. An instruction or a shorter lifetime leaves the extra permissions usable.

items.lesson_title: Securing Recursive Chains through Robust De-provisioning
items.stem: A vendor-onboarding agent is compromised. Its access token has already been revoked. Two partner services still recognize its registered identity, and a helper still has a delegated grant. The incident lead wants to prevent new access after the current credentials expire. What should the team do next?

options.a: De-provision the agent across both partners and remove the helper’s derived grant.
options.b: Wait for the old access token to expire and leave the registrations in place.
options.c: Replace the agent’s token while keeping the same partner registrations and helper grant.
options.d: Revoke the helper’s current token and retain the agent’s partner registrations.

items.rationale: Revocation addressed the current token. The remaining partner registrations can still confer new access. De-provisioning removes the compromised identity and its associated access across the partners, including the surviving grant derived from it.
